Study Warns Misleading Artificial Intelligence Buzzwords Distort Public Understanding and Accountability

A Simon Fraser University study published in the peer-reviewed journal AI and Ethics warns that industry-led artificial intelligence jargon may be distorting public comprehension of the technology while obscuring its tangible harms. The authors introduce the term glosslighting to describe how tech companies deploy specialized glossaries to manipulate public perception, evade scrutiny, and promote the questionable assumption that increasingly powerful systems are inevitable.

Led by assistant professor of computing science Nicholas Vincent, alongside undergraduate student Ayana Hussain and doctoral candidate Weina Jin, the research team analyzed how current language misrepresents algorithmic functions. Vincent observed that the language surrounding artificial intelligence has become deliberately confusing, creating widespread misunderstandings that have progressively worsened rather than improved over time.

The researchers specifically criticized anthropomorphic expressions such as AI hallucinations, co-pilot, and agentic systems. Such framing attributes human-like qualities to automated software, encouraging observers to view inaccurate outputs as simple human-style mistakes rather than recognizing false information as systemic, corporate errors that require institutional accountability.

The study also demonstrates how benign technical metaphors conceal significant physical and environmental costs. For instance, referring to remote data storage as the cloud sidesteps the operational reality that user information is processed in controversial, energy-intensive data centers and massive server installations that consume substantial local water supplies.

Behind the polished rhetoric of seamless intelligence, the authors emphasize the presence of human labor and material impacts that corporate messaging obscures. The study highlights poorly compensated content moderators who review traumatic material, local communities whose resources are drawn upon to sustain server infrastructure, and citizens whose daily lives are governed by probabilistic scoring systems misleadingly labeled as solutions.

The authors also categorized speculative phrasing such as superintelligence, frontier AI, artificial general intelligence, and existential risk as diversions. According to the findings, focusing public and policy debates on distant, hypothetical future dangers effectively distracts society from pressing contemporary concerns, labor practices, and immediate socioeconomic disruptions.

Corporate claims regarding democratizing AI, open AI, and ethical systems were similarly evaluated as misleading public relations tactics. The paper notes that these terms project an impression of decentralized control while technical power remains heavily concentrated within a small circle of dominant commercial entities, framing structural challenges as narrow technical puzzles rather than topics for open civic debate.

To counter these distortions, the authors urge researchers, media professionals, and the public to adopt rigorous and differentiated descriptions for distinct technologies. Vincent pointed out that a basic search engine operates fundamentally differently from a chatbot, a recommendation model, or a vision system steering an autonomous vehicle, arguing that everyone impacted by these tools deserves precise explanations of what they are and how they function.

Beyond anthropomorphic analogies, the researchers documented how technical jargon can depoliticize critical policy questions by presenting societal challenges as purely engineering matters. Phrases such as deep learning, bias, ex ante risk regulation, and data subjects often frame systemic issues as overly technical or inaccessible, which the authors observe discourages broader public debate regarding whether certain technologies should be deployed at all. Similarly, industry buzzwords including data mining, scaling, and human-in-the-loop obscure the ongoing environmental and social burdens generated by operating large software architectures. Marketing concepts such as smart city, AI superpower, and race to AI, alongside invocations of robot rights, further divert scrutiny away from the corporate actors directing system behavior by redirecting public focus toward speculative competition and future possibilities. Complementary labels like responsible AI, collaborative AI, and human-centric AI allow tech enterprises to brand themselves as trustworthy while real authority remains tightly held.

To replace these misleading descriptors, the study provides clearer substitute terms designed to restore accountability. The authors note that while most of their recommended alternatives immediately simplify communication, others inevitably require additional context and nuance. Vincent stressed that when subjects involve genuine complexity, institutions and communicators bear an inherent responsibility to invest the necessary effort to help audiences comprehend the mechanisms at work. Furthermore, Vincent anticipates that shifting market dynamics will reinforce this need for transparency. As consumers become more discerning, commercial buyers and the general public will increasingly demand explicit functional details rather than vague promises, meaning companies marketing costly tools will need to offer precise explanations of what their products actually execute.

The research initiative also highlighted the benefits of uniting contributors from different career milestones within academia, pairing an undergraduate student, a doctoral candidate, and a faculty member. For Hussain, translating grassroots anxieties and everyday online discussions into a peer-reviewed investigation represented an opportunity to clarify how artificial intelligence is framed across the media, academia, and commercial enterprise. Jin emphasized that this collaborative analysis underlined the urgent necessity for scientific precision, cautioning that researchers must communicate their discoveries with methodological rigor and avoid exaggerating software capabilities. Vincent affirmed the value of this multi-tier dynamic, remarking that student leadership serves a vital role in holding established academic institutions to account.

The peer-reviewed paper, titled AI still has a vocabulary problem: toward terminological accountability in artificial intelligence, was formally released on October 16, 2026. Through their catalog of deceptive vocabulary, the authors advocate for disciplined linguistic standards that demystify algorithmic tools and ensure that the corporations developing them answer directly for their real-world consequences.

Subject of Research: Linguistic analysis of artificial intelligence terminology and its impact on public accountability

Article Title: ​‘Glosslighting’ the public: SFU study calls for overhaul of industry-led AI buzzwords
